shared_context.content: For a positive integer d and integers u,v, define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|.
shared_context.label: Interval divisibility count

shared_context.content: For an integer b >= 0, write S_b for the polynomial ring Q[y_1,...,y_b] with weighted grading deg(y_i)=i for 1 <= i <= b. When b=0, this means S_0 = Q.
shared_context.label: Initial interval weighted polynomial ring

shared_context.content: For integers 0 <= a <= b, write I_{a,b} := {a+1,...,b} and R_{a,b} := Q[x_s : s in I_{a,b}] with weighted grading deg(x_s)=s. When a=b, this means R_{a,b} = Q.
shared_context.label: Target weighted polynomial ring on an interval

shared_context.content: A sequence u_1,...,u_n in a commutative ring A is regular if for each i the image of u_i is a non-zero-divisor in A/(u_1,...,u_{i-1}) and the final quotient A/(u_1,...,u_n) is nonzero. The empty sequence is regular.
shared_context.label: Regular sequence

strategy_summary: Embed the target ring R = Q[x_s : s in {a+1,...,b}] into the larger weighted polynomial ring S = Q[y_1,...,y_b] by viewing R as the quotient S/(y_1,...,y_a). Package the desired tail degrees together with the killed coordinate degrees into the ordered list (1,2,...,a,r+a+1,...,r+b). The given interval divisibility hypothesis is exactly the divisor-count dominance needed for a stronger existence theorem in the initial-interval ring S. After obtaining a regular sequence in S of those degrees, straighten the first a entries to y_1,...,y_a by a graded triangular automorphism, then descend the remaining entries to the quotient ring R.
